intro: Every day you make choices. Sleep in or eat breakfast? Spend your birthday money or save it? Join the team or the club? You cannot have everything, because time and money run out. That simple fact is where economics begins. This unit gives you a way of thinking that economists use to make sense of choices, big and small.

First you will look at choices up close: scarcity, the four factors of production, opportunity cost, thinking one step at a time, and the incentives that push people one way or another. Then you will zoom out to whole countries. Every society must decide what to make, how to make it and who gets it. You will compare traditional, command, market and mixed economies, and see where the United States fits.

By the end, you will be able to name the opportunity cost of a choice, score options on a decision grid, predict how people react to an incentive, and explain how different economic systems answer the same three questions. These are tools you can use at the kitchen table, at school and as a voter.
bigQuestion: How do people and whole societies decide what to do with things that are scarce?

timeline.t: Adam Smith publishes The Wealth of Nations, describing markets and self-interest
David Ricardo explains comparative advantage and why trade helps both sides
Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels publish The Communist Manifesto
Alfred Marshall publishes Principles of Economics, spreading marginal thinking
Congress creates the Federal Reserve, with a Reserve Bank in Chicago
The Soviet Union is formed and later builds a command economy
The Social Security Act creates a safety net for older Americans
Korea is divided; North and South later choose different systems
China begins market reforms, letting farmers sell crops in markets
The Soviet Union breaks apart and its countries move toward markets

words.d: the basic problem that people's wants are greater than the limited resources available to meet them
the resources used to make goods and services: land, labor, capital and entrepreneurship
tools, machines and buildings made by people and used to produce other goods and services
the value of the next-best choice you give up when you make a decision
giving up some of one thing to get more of another; all the options not chosen
the extra benefit from doing or having one more unit of something
a reward or cost that encourages or discourages a certain choice
an economic system where customs passed down through generations answer the economic questions
an economic system where the central government owns most resources and makes the main economic decisions
an economic system where individuals and private businesses own resources and make decisions through buying and selling
an economic system that combines private markets with some government decision-making
the legal rights to own, use and sell things, including land, goods and ideas

test.q: Which best explains why every society must make economic choices?
choices: Resources are limited but wants are not
test.why: Scarcity forces every society to choose.

test.q: A worker who assembles bikes is which factor of production?
test.why: Human work and skill is labor.

test.q: You rank a paid job first, a pool party second and a movie third. You take the job. What is your opportunity cost?
test.why: Opportunity cost is only the next-best option: the pool party.

test.q: A camp is free but you give up 25 hours of work at $12 an hour (example). What is the money part of the opportunity cost?
Extra study hours add 8, 5, 3 and 1 points (example). What is the total gain after 3 hours?
In that same study example, the value of rest is 4 points per hour. How many hours should you study?
test.why: Hours 1 and 2 add more than 4 points. Hour 3 adds 3, which is less than 4, so stop at 2.

test.q: A city fines people $100 for littering (example). What kind of incentive is this?
test.why: A fine is a penalty that discourages an action.

test.q: A decision grid gives Option A scores of 4, 3 and 5, and Option B scores of 2, 5 and 4. Which wins?
A prize per book read leads students to pick very short books. What is this?
test.why: The incentive produced a result nobody planned.

test.q: In which system do custom and habit answer the economic questions?
test.why: A traditional economy relies on customs passed down over time.

test.q: Planners make 80,000 loaves, but people want 95,000 at the set price (example). What is the shortage?
In a market economy, what mainly tells producers what to make?
choices: Prices set by buyers and sellers
test.why: Prices signal what buyers want and what sellers will offer.

test.q: Why do private businesses rarely build lighthouses or streetlights?
choices: They cannot easily charge each user
test.why: Public goods are hard to keep people from using, so it is hard to charge them.

test.q: Which describes the United States economy?
test.why: Most decisions are made in private markets, with some government role.

test.q: North and South Korea started with similar land and people. What mainly explains their different incomes today?
test.why: Economists point to different systems, incentives and property rights.

write.prompt: Your town has $50,000 (example) and must choose: fix the park playground or add a free after-school bus. Use a decision grid, name the opportunity cost, say what incentives each choice creates, and argue which the town should pick. Name the trade-off.
tips: Name the opportunity cost: the one option the town gives up.
Show your numbers in a small decision grid with at least 3 criteria.
Name one incentive each choice creates and how people may respond.
Admit the trade-off: say what the losing side still has going for it.
